Summary:

This is an interesting paper that contains a very valuable comparison of neuronal performance in binocular vision between two visual areas, one (V5/MT) in the dorsal stream and the other (V4) in the ventral stream. The paper builds upon a number of previous findings from this research group and others using the technique of testing binocular visual neurons with inputs that vary from being strongly correlated between left and right eyes' images (random dot stereograms, RDS) to complete anti-correlation (anti-random dot stereograms, aRDS). The prediction is that neurons in V4 behave in a match-based way and MT in a correlation-based way (aRDS produces inversion in curve correlation). The data support this prediction well. That is, V4 neurons show greatly reduced “negative part” of the tuning curve, consistent with a non-linear exclusion operation. MT neurons, in contrast, exhibit robust negative parts of the tuning curves, similar to responses of V1 neurons. The results suggest significant differences in the visual processing of binocular information in the two areas.

The results compare the response to two different ways of manipulating the binocular correlation structure of images. The first varies from correlated (+1) to anticorrelated (-1) by replacing some dot pairs in matched locations in the left and right eyes with dots placed at randomly chosen locations in the left and right eyes. With this manipulation, as dots in matched locations are replaced by dots in randomly chosen locations, the correlation level of two images falls away from +1 and -1, eventually approaching 0 when all dots are in randomly chosen locations. In the second manipulation, dots remain in their matched locations but the proportion of them that are correlated or anticorrelated is varied. This manipulation arrives at an interesting combination of dots which is half correlated and half anticorrelated: the average correlation of such a figure is zero, but the structural distribution of correlations is different from the previous manipulation in which randomly chosen dot locations are applied. The authors exploit this and call this second stimulus half-matched, because half of the dots have positive correlation and the signal from these dots leads to a perceptual sense of depth, whereas there is no specific depth apparent when the images are binocularly uncorrelated by placing dots in random locations.

For both these types of stimulus with an average of zero correlation, the response of an idealized detector of binocular correlation (such as the Ohzawa, DeAngelis and Freeman model) would naturally be zero in both cases. However, as the authors recognize, the slightest non-linearity in neural processing would lead to different responses to these two stimuli. Therefore, the authors have devised a way of assessing the responses to these two stimuli across the whole range of correlation values. This is helpful and presents some interesting findings.

Essential revisions:

1) Area-ratio measure: A major concern is that not every aspect of the data will have been captured by the new area-ratio measure. The issue is the relationship between signed-amplitude ratio and binocular correlation (as sketched in Figure 4A of the submitted paper). The assumption of the paper is that this is always monotonic as a function of correlation, but there are already clear published examples where this is not true (Figure 1A of Krug et al., 2004 is one example). In this case, the relationship between signed-amplitude ratio and binocular correlation would be V-shaped and nonlinear, not monotonic and linear as shown in Figure 4A). So, the empirical question would be whether the data-sets for this paper contain any signs of this non-linear relationship.

2) Symmetry: (a) The main finding here is that the disparity tuning symmetry is correlated with the disparity representation in both MT and V4. More specifically, neurons with even-symmetric tuning tended to have match-based representations and neurons with odd-symmetric tuning tended to have correlation-based representations. Although the correlation was rather robust in MT (r = 0.55), in V4 this correlation was weak (r = 0.34). The authors should acknowledge the fact that tuning symmetry could only explain 11% of the variance in the disparity representation metric (the area ratio). Maybe the correlation coefficient did not capture the nonlinear relationship between the two metrics in V4, and therefore other ways to quantify this relationship should be considered. (b) The authors spend a section in the Discussion on response symmetry. However, it is not clear what the functional significance of this finding is (beyond the obvious). What new offered by the symmetry finding? "neurons with even-symmetric tuning preferentially constituted the neural solution to the correspondence problem in extrastriate areas." Is this surprising? Somehow the message did not come through.

3) Novelty and significance: Precisely what new has been learned here? This must be spelled out clearly. One gets the impression that the main observations in this study are not new. The authors themselves published work on V4 (some of these data were used in this study), and Krug et al., 2003 described the responses of MT neurons to anticorrelated disparity. (Possibly the only difference being the MT neurons with an area ratio of 1, which were described in Krug et al. but were almost absent in this study.) Perhaps the most novel aspect of this study is the use of traditional ventral pathway stimulus (static RDS and aRDS stimuli) for dorsal pathway study. These results (fast robust response) serve to further support the view of MT/dorsal pathway in action vision. The V4 findings, while well conducted, do not significantly change or extend our view of V4 function in binocular disparity.

4) Overstated conclusions: (a) The conclusion that the data demonstrate “a general principle of the stereoscopic system both within and across the dorsal and ventral pathways” seems too strong based on this study in only two areas. For this conclusion, we need data in many other areas. Nevertheless, I also acknowledge that this will not be easy because most visual areas contain either a strongly match-based representation (such as inferotemporal cortex and parietal areas AIP), or a correlation-based representation such as V1 and V2. (b) Similarly, the conclusion that “neurons with even-symmetric tuning preferentially constituted the neural solution to the correspondence problem in extrastriate areas” seems too general. (c) The authors statement that “the correlation-based disparity signals in MT directly contribute to some aspects of depth perception” is too strong since the behavioral effects of microstimulation in MT could have been caused by the match-based neurons alone (since microstimulation does not discriminate between the two types of neurons).

5) Visual eccentricities of recordings in V4 and MT: The mean eccentricities of the V4 neurons are ~9 deg while that of MT neurons are ~7 deg. This seems rather eccentric for V4. Do these findings hold for RFs in more central (0-3 deg) eccentricity? This is important as V4's primary function is in central vision.

claims.source: As binocular disparity is used for both 'what' (object vision) and 'where' (spatial vision) functions, the visual system processes binocular disparity along both the dorsal and ventral pathways (Neri, 2005; Orban et al., 2006; Parker, 2007; Roe et al., 2012; Welchman, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on disparity processing in both pathways.

claims.claim: To encode binocular disparity faithfully, the visual system should identify corresponding visual features in left and right retinal images.
claims.source: To encode binocular disparity faithfully in accordance with the geometry of the 3D world, the visual system should identify the corresponding visual features in left and right retinal images that originate from the same surface point in the 3D space (Julesz, 1971; Marr and Poggio, 1976; Marr and Poggio, 1979).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work on the stereo correspondence problem.

claims.claim: Anticorrelated random-dot stereograms (aRDSs) are used to probe the neuronal process for stereo correspondence.
claims.source: A conventional method to probe the neuronal process for stereo correspondence is to measure the disparity selectivity for anticorrelated random-dot stereograms (aRDSs) (Chen et al., 2017; Cumming and Parker, 1997; Goncalves and Welchman, 2017; Janssen et al., 2003; Krug et al., 2004; Kumano et al., 2008; Nieder and Wagner, 2001; Ohzawa, 1998; Samonds et al., 2013; Takemura et al., 2001; Tanabe et al., 2004; Theys et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations to previous studies using aRDSs to study stereo correspondence.

claims.claim: In aRDSs, one eye image is contrast-reversed to eliminate the natural solution to the correspondence problem.
claims.source: In aRDSs, one eye image is contrast-reversed to eliminate the natural solution to the correspondence problem; the natural solution requires the depth of the corresponding points to vary smoothly over space, but such a solution does not exist for aRDSs.
claims.evidence: This is a standard explanation of how aRDSs work, based on established knowledge in vision science.

claims.claim: Many V1 neurons falsely encode the disparity embedded in aRDSs.
claims.source: Although the activity of many V1 neurons encodes binocular disparity, these neurons also falsely encode the disparity embedded in aRDSs (Cumming and Parker, 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study demonstrating this property of V1 neurons.

claims.claim: Simple computations akin to interocular cross-correlation explain the primitive disparity representation in V1.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a foundational study on the disparity energy model.

results.result: MT and V4 are mid-tier stages of the dorsal and ventral pathways that both causally contribute to stereoscopic depth judgment.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 establish the anatomical and functional context for the study based on well-established prior literature. The citations to multiple previous studies (DeAngelis et al., 1998; Shiozaki et al., 2012; Uka and DeAngelis, 2006) provide strong support for these foundational claims about MT and V4's roles in stereoscopic processing.

results.result: The study recorded from 83 disparity-selective neurons in MT and 78 in V4 using random-dot stereograms with graded anticorrelation, with appropriate ethical approval and experimental design.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 and C64-C72 describe the experimental methodology, sample sizes, and ethical approvals. These are directly stated methodological facts that are internally consistent and appropriately documented. The use of one monkey (Monkey O) for both MT and V4 recordings (C67) provides valuable within-subject control.

results.result: MT neurons showed characteristic correlation-based disparity representation with U-shaped selectivity patterns and tuning inversion at negative correlations, while V4 neurons lacked these features and showed match-based representation patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 describe population-level differences between MT and V4 in their responses to graded anticorrelation stimuli. The statistical analyses (binomial tests, Kruskal-Wallis tests) are appropriate and the results show clear qualitative differences: MT shows 75-78% tuning inversion at -100% and -70% correlation (C29-C30) with significant p-values, while V4 shows gradual decrease without surpassing chance levels (C32). The data in Figure 3 support these claims.

results.result: The area ratio (a novel metric quantifying disparity representation type) was significantly higher in MT (median 0.50) than V4 (median 0.17), while the conventional amplitude ratio showed no difference between areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 present the key quantitative finding using both a novel metric (area ratio) and conventional metric (amplitude ratio). The statistical tests are appropriate (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Mann-Whitney U-test) with highly significant p-values for area ratio differences (p=3.6×10⁻⁴) but non-significant for amplitude ratio (p=0.47). This demonstrates that the novel graded anticorrelation approach reveals differences not detectable with conventional methods. Figure 5 and supplementary analyses (Figure 5—figure supplements 3-4) provide strong support.

results.result: Disparity-tuning symmetry predicted the type of disparity representation both within and across MT and V4, with even-symmetric neurons showing more match-based representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 and C7-C8 establish a fundamental relationship between tuning shape and representation type. The correlations are statistically significant in both areas (MT: rs=0.41, p=1.4×10⁻³; V4: rs=0.34, p=0.025) and V4 neurons have more even-symmetric tuning than MT (C7, Figure 7). However, the moderate correlation coefficients and modest R² values (24% for MT, 20% for V4, Figure 6—figure supplement 2) indicate that tuning symmetry explains only part of the variance, which the authors appropriately acknowledge.

results.result: MT transmitted disparity signals faster (78 ms vs 101 ms latency) and more robustly (peak sDDI 0.18 vs 0.13) than V4, representing a 29% latency advantage and 28% strength advantage.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 and C3-C4 demonstrate MT's advantage in signaling speed and strength using time-resolved analysis of disparity selectivity. The cumulative Gaussian fitting approach is appropriate, bootstrap statistics confirm significance (p=0.0083 for latency, p<1.0×10⁻⁴ for amplitude), and the results are shown in Figure 8. This finding is particularly notable given that the stimuli were designed for V4 (non-moving RDSs), potentially underestimating MT's advantage.

results.result: Mean eccentricity differed between MT (6.9°) and V4 (9.0°), but area ratio showed no correlation with eccentricity in either area.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C73-C74 address a potential confound. The eccentricity difference between areas is documented (C43), but correlation analyses show no relationship between eccentricity and area ratio in either MT (rs=-0.035, p=0.79) or V4 (rs=-0.065, p=0.68). This suggests the MT-V4 differences are not simply due to eccentricity differences, though the authors appropriately note limitations in detecting such relationships given the eccentricity range sampled.

results.result: Computational modeling showed that the threshold energy model produces more match-based representations when relative receptive field size is smaller, with area ratio monotonically increasing with RF size.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 describe simulation results shown in Figure 9. The threshold energy model simulations systematically varied relative RF size and demonstrated the predicted relationship between RF size and representation type. This provides mechanistic insight into how the match-based representation could arise from correlation-based mechanisms through nonlinearity, though the authors appropriately note this is not a complete explanation.

results.result: MT may consist of two groups of neurons (match-based and intermediate), while V4 lacks the intermediate group, based on potentially bimodal vs unimodal area ratio distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 propose a bimodal distribution in MT versus unimodal in V4. However, the bimodality test was not significant (Hartigan's dip test: p=0.24, C46), and the authors acknowledge uncertainty with 'might.' The bootstrap analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) shows two clusters for MT but this is not definitive. The quantile-quantile plots (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) suggest MT follows normal distribution and V4 follows exponential distribution within the interquartile range, which is more consistent with different unimodal distributions than bimodality.

results.result: The division of labor between dorsal and ventral pathways embodies a tradeoff between rapid/robust signal transmission (dorsal/MT) and complex computation for elaborate representations (ventral/V4).
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C75 synthesize the experimental findings into a broader theoretical framework. This interpretation is well-supported by the convergent evidence: MT shows faster/stronger but more primitive signals (C3-C4, C38-C42), while V4 shows slower/weaker but more sophisticated signals (C5, C33-C34). The tradeoff interpretation logically follows from the data, though it remains an interpretation rather than a directly tested hypothesis.

results.result: MT's fast, robust correlation-based disparity signals likely contribute to rapid vergence eye movements, coarse depth perception, and urgent depth judgments, consistent with prior psychophysical and physiological findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C57 connect the current findings to functional roles based on extensive prior literature. The speculation about MT's role (C48-C49, C54) is appropriately qualified and supported by citations to relevant studies on vergence (C55-C56), perceptual judgment (C50-C51), and disparity magnitude effects (C52-C53). The consistency with absolute disparity coding (C57) strengthens the interpretation. While speculative, these claims are well-grounded in converging evidence.

results.result: V4 is in the middle of solving the correspondence problem along the ventral pathway, contributing to fine depth perception, 3D shape encoding, and relative disparity representation, as supported by prior causal and physiological studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 interpret V4's role based on current findings and prior literature. The interpretation that V4 is 'in the middle' of solving correspondence (C58-C59) is supported by the observation that V4 neurons show intermediate properties. The functional roles are well-supported by citations to prior studies showing choice-predictive responses (C60), microstimulation effects (C61), relative disparity coding (C62), and 3D shape selectivity (C63). This provides a coherent framework for understanding V4's contribution.

results.result: Background claims establish that both dorsal and ventral pathways process binocular disparity, that disparity requires solving the correspondence problem, and that V1 neurons show primitive correlation-based representations that falsely encode anticorrelated stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C21 provide essential background from established literature. These are well-supported by appropriate citations to foundational studies and represent accepted knowledge in the field. They establish the theoretical framework and motivation for the current study. No issues with these background claims are apparent.

results.result: Vision for action may depend more on the dorsal pathway due to benefits from rapid transmission, while color and object analysis may depend more on the ventral pathway due to requirements for complex computation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 extend the tradeoff interpretation to broader theories of dorsal/ventral function. While speculative (appropriately qualified with 'may'), these claims provide a unifying framework connecting the current findings to established theories (Goodale and Milner, 1992; Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982). The speculation is reasonable given the data, though it goes beyond what was directly tested.
